title: B2B Gifting: +150% Qualified Leads on the Same Budget
excerpt: Restructuring paid search for a corporate gifting brand lifted conversion rates 50% and qualified leads 150% with no extra spend. Read the case.
rm_desc: A paid search account restructure lifted qualified leads 150% on the same budget. Read the case.
content: This paid search account restructure covers a premium B2B corporate-gifting brand selling globally, with an account spending real money against queries that were never going to buy.
How the paid search account restructure worked

The account was restructured in full around high-intent queries, moving budget from wasted queries to buying ones while total spend held flat. Match-type and negative-keyword discipline kept the new structure clean, and measurement ran on cost per qualified lead, never on impressions or clicks.
What the account looked like before the restructure

Broad match on category terms with a thin negative-keyword list, a common pattern in accounts that were set up quickly and never revisited. Impressions and clicks looked healthy on a surface-level dashboard, which is exactly what made the underlying waste invisible without a proper paid search account restructure: the account was spending, and spending looks like activity, even when very little of it was reaching a buyer with actual purchase intent.
Conversion rates rose 50% and qualified leads grew 150% on the same budget. The money moved from wasted queries to buying ones.

Gains this size are what fixing a poorly structured account looks like. A well-run account improves in single digits, and anyone promising 150% on top of good work is promising arithmetic that does not exist. A paid search account restructure only produces numbers like this once, on the account's worst starting point; the job after that is holding the gain, not repeating it.
How to tell if your account needs the same fix

A few tells worth checking before commissioning a full paid search account restructure: broad match keywords with a negative list under a few dozen terms, conversion tracking that counts form starts rather than qualified submissions, and a cost-per-click that looks reasonable next to Google's own Keyword Planner estimate but a cost-per-lead nobody has actually calculated. Any one of those on its own is a fix; two or three together usually means the account needs a full restructure rather than incremental tuning.

This engagement sat inside our paid media service; the full scope of what a paid search account restructure typically includes is documented there. Brands suspecting their own account has the same underlying structural problem can start with an audit before committing to a full engagement.
What changed in the negative keyword list

Before the restructure, the negative keyword list ran to a few dozen obvious exclusions, competitor brand names, unrelated product categories. After, it ran to several hundred, built by mining several months of search-term reports for queries that had spent money without ever converting. That expanded negative list did more to protect the budget than any single positive keyword addition, since it stopped continuous, quiet spend leakage on queries that looked plausible but never converted, month after month, without anyone noticing until the reports were actually mined properly.
Why the same restructure is not always the answer

A paid search account restructure only unlocks a gain this size when the starting account has structural waste to remove. An account that is already well-negatived, properly segmented by intent and tracked against qualified leads rather than raw conversions will not see anything close to 150%, because there is no equivalent waste left to redirect. Asking for a proper diagnostic before signing any restructure engagement is really the only honest way to know for certain which of those two situations an account is actually in.
